name: Alphonse Conway
bio: A Worthing boy — son of a widow who let lodgings, keen to go to sea — whom Wilde and Douglas met launching a boat on the beach in August 1894; for six weeks he was, in Wilde's contemporaneous letter, 'my only companion,' sailing to Littlehampton and bathing with Wilde, and receiving an inscribed cigarette case, a photograph, a novel, a walking-stick and a blue serge suit before the twenty-four-hour Brighton trip of about 27 September. Queensberry's plea alleged solicitation and gross indecency at Worthing and the Albion Hotel, Brighton; the allegation, outside the Central Criminal Court's jurisdiction, was never charged, and Conway — seen outside the Court in May 1895 — never testified.
bio_sources: Wilde's libel-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 137-139 (djvu OCR)
Wilde's final-trial cross-examination, Hyde, Trials (1948), pp. 318-319 (djvu OCR)
Queensberry's plea, Hyde, Trials (1948), p. 344 (IIIF page image 2026-08-03)

Wilde to Lord Alfred Douglas [August 1894], Complete Letters (2000), p. 602, with the editors' note 'Alphonse Conway, a newspaper boy whom Wilde had met on the beach at Worthing' (p. 602 n 5; read at rendered PDF p. 654, 2026-08-03)

Antony Edmonds, Oscar Wilde's Scandalous Summer (2014), extract at oscarwilde.org.uk - 1891 baptism record giving 10 July 1878; Richard Wood, 'The Later Fate of Alphonse Conway', oscarwilde.org.uk - argued identification with Harold Payne, d. 15 Jan. 1915
bio_note: No birth/death dates found in sources read so far, and NO AGE appears in the plea as printed by Hyde (verified in the source image): Wilde on oath estimated 'a youth of about eighteen,' the Letters editors call him 'a newspaper boy' (undated), and Wilde denied he sold papers. The ROSTER's 'aged 16 (plea)' note is NOT supported by the sources read so far — the 16 figure presumably derives from the uncensored libel transcript (Holland, Irish Peacock, 2003, not consulted); flagged for verification there. BIRTH YEAR FOUND (added 2026-08-03, web): 1878. Antony Edmonds, Oscar Wilde's Scandalous Summer: The 1894 Worthing Holiday and the Aftermath (Amberley, 2014), in the extract from the book reproduced on the author's own site oscarwilde.org.uk (page 'Further Information about Alphonse Conway's Origins', read so far), states: 'A document has recently become available that gives Alphonse's date of birth. This is the record at St Andrew's Church, Worthing of the boy's baptism on 28 March 1891, which records his date of birth as 10 July 1878. He was thus twelve years old when he was belatedly baptised, and about six weeks past his sixteenth birthday when he met Wilde.' Edmonds corroborates the year from the April 1891 census, where Sarah Conway's son 'Alphus', born at Bognor, is twelve. WHY THE YEAR ONLY, AND NO DAY: three documents give three different days and this record does not choose between them - the 1891 baptism register 10 July 1878; the birth certificate (found by Edmund Marlowe, reported on the same page, registering 'Alfonso Conway White Payne' at Bognor to Julia Sarah Payne) 13 July 1878, which Edmonds thinks is probably the registration date entered in error; and a Royal Navy service record 14 July 1878, which only applies if the identification below holds. Conflict reported, not resolved. DEATH: STILL NULL, WITH A STRONG BUT ARGUED LEAD. Richard Wood, 'The Later Fate of Alphonse Conway' (oscarwilde.org.uk, published there at Edmonds's invitation, read so far), argues that Conway took his mother's registered surname and his own baptismal middle name and lived thereafter as Harold Payne: a Royal Navy Sick Berth Steward, born Bognor 1878, mother Sarah J. Payne, who enlisted 2 July 1900, was invalided out with tuberculosis in November 1914 and 'died in Portsmouth shortly afterwards, on 15 January 1915, aged only 36', buried in Kingston cemetery, Portsmouth. Wood builds this from census, birth, service, death and probate records and calls it 'surely beyond sheer coincidence'; it is nonetheless an argued identification rather than a record naming the trial witness, so no death date is entered here and the call is left open. Two things in the repo record corroborate the name-change premise independently: Queensberry's plea as printed by Hyde names him 'Alfonso Harold Conway' - the middle name Wood's argument turns on - and the Letters editors call him 'Alphonse Conway, a newspaper boy whom Wilde had met on the beach at Worthing' (p. 602 n. 5). AGE AT TRIAL, UNCHANGED: Wilde swore he was 'about eighteen'; the baptism date makes him sixteen in August 1894, which is Edmonds's point and is the likely origin of the widely repeated 16. SWEEP FOR DATES, 2026-08-03 (what was searched): the Complete Letters (2000) OCR mirror plus the General Index; McKenna, The Secret Life of Oscar Wilde (2008), repo PDF; Murray, Bosie (2020), repo PDF; Frankel, The Unrepentant Years (2017), repo PDF; Hyde, The Trials of Oscar Wilde, in the Internet Archive copy (item in.ernet.dli.2015.499238, OCR text downloaded and searched, key pages then read as page images); and the open web.
